title: I Posted the Powder-Coat Oven Hours After They Left My Hooks

parts.text: I stepped into oven one at 2:03 p.m. and lead Kade was already using my numbered hooks. The board said: SEVENTY MINUTES. HOOKS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-five, finish steward, holding a clipboard that listed our cure. Kade shrugged. "Leads keep the oven." I photographed the board, the booking, and his parts on my hooks. Then I asked for the oven hours. At 2:11 the coat desk pinged why Kade's parts sat on our hooks. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The coat desk can see Kade's parts in oven one during our cure.

social.video_title: He left his parts on my numbered hooks — Part 1/2
social.description: Powder-coat oven, a lead on my hooks, a seventy-minute clock he posted. I logged the parts. Would you have asked for the oven hours?

parts.text: Kade called it flash-off until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the oven still. The hooks went back to my numbered rail. Kade ran a slot of their own and told the next lead atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: LEADS DO NOT KEEP THE OVEN. I keep our cure on a labeled card. Kade brown-bags his parts. The oven finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Leads do not keep the oven — Part 2/2
social.description: Oven hours, numbered hooks, and a second line on the board. Was flash-off ever our cure?
